# snowglobe

> snowglobe is a Go CLI that turns a Docker image into a static website that runs it in the
> browser: real Linux on a 64-bit ARM CPU emulated in WebAssembly (armless), restored from a
> snapshot taken once the app was ready. The output is a folder of static files (GitHub Pages
> works); no server runs the program. The same site also runs headlessly from the command line,
> in a container or natively with no Docker (the emulator sandboxes itself), as a single
> executable, and as a sandbox that agents and job runners drive, on machines without KVM.
> Guests must be arm64 Alpine images (FROM alpine, built for arm64, or FROM arm64v8/alpine).

Live demos: https://filipecabaco.github.io/snowglobe/ (Supabase, Elixir IEx, PostgreSQL,
Elixir + Postgres, Python + Rich, TypeScript + Zod, Go + Bubble Tea, Rust + clap, Java + Gson,
curl + jq). Docs: https://filipecabaco.github.io/snowglobe/docs/ (guides and the full CLI
reference). Source: https://github.com/filipecabaco/snowglobe

Install: a release binary (Linux or macOS, amd64 or arm64) from
https://github.com/filipecabaco/snowglobe/releases, or
`go install github.com/filipecabaco/snowglobe/cmd/snowglobe@latest`.

## Commands

- `snowglobe build <dir with a Dockerfile | image ref | image archive> [flags]` builds the site
  into `--out` (default `dist`). With Docker by default; `--builder native` (or
  `SNOWGLOBE_BUILDER=native`) needs no Docker: it pulls the image from its registry (Docker Hub,
  GHCR, any registry serving public images) or reads a `docker save` / OCI layout archive.
- `snowglobe serve [dir] [--port N]` previews a built site on localhost.
- `snowglobe pool <dir>` makes every site under a directory share one content-addressed blob store.
- `snowglobe pwa <site> [--name N] [--short-name N]` makes a built site an installable Progressive
  Web App that works offline once it has run. Run it after `pool`.
- `snowglobe pack <site> [-o site.tar.gz]` writes a site as one self-contained tarball (.tar.gz or
  .tar.zst, pooled blobs included) to publish on a CDN.
- `snowglobe run [site] [--name N] [--detach] [--runtime docker|native]` restores a built site
  headlessly. `docker` (the default) is a sandboxed container (unprivileged, read-only,
  memory-capped, offline unless built with a network); `native` (or `SNOWGLOBE_RUNTIME=native`, and
  whenever there is no Docker) runs snowglobe-vm here, which sandboxes itself: no_new_privs,
  Landlock and seccomp on Linux, Seatbelt on macOS. In a terminal it is an interactive session
  (ctrl-] quits); with stdin piped, each line is typed in as a command and the output printed as
  plain text. The site can be a directory, a tarball, a tarball URL, or a deployed site's URL
  (e.g. https://filipecabaco.github.io/snowglobe/python/), fetched into a local cache first.
  Native instances of one site share its snapshot's memory: the first writes it to an image in
  the cache (`ram/`, one per snapshot, named by its hash) and every instance maps it
  copy-on-write, so pages no instance writes are held once and a restore takes a few
  milliseconds (Linux: ~46 MB PSS per Python instance instead of ~111 MB).
  `SNOWGLOBE_RAM_IMAGE=off` restores into memory of the instance's own.
  - `-p HOST:GUEST` (repeatable) forwards a host port to a guest port (127.0.0.1 unless
    IP:HOST:GUEST); needs a site built with `--network fetch`.
  - `--max-runtime DURATION` ends the run after that long (exit 124); `--stop-file PATH` ends it
    once PATH exists (exit 143). Either way the job running in the guest is killed first.
  - `--log-dir DIR` keeps durable logs: `console.log` (the app's terminal), `serial.log` (kernel
    messages, the job shell) and `events.jsonl` (start, restored, job_start, job_end, stop; one
    JSON object a line). Named native instances log to the user cache's `snowglobe/logs/<name>`.
  - `--tunnel [HOST:]PORT=URL`, `--tunnel-token URL`, `--allow-private`, `--record-reads FILE`.
  - `--fork` (with `--detach --name`, native) makes the instance a template: it restores once,
    and every `snowglobe sh` on it runs in a fresh copy of the machine, forked in milliseconds and
    sharing its memory. Nothing one command does is seen by the next; `sh` is all it takes.
- `snowglobe exec <name> <command>` types one command into a running instance's app and prints
  only what it printed (plain text when piped): the way to drive a REPL.
- `snowglobe sh <name> [--json] [--timeout SECS] '<command>'` runs a shell command, passed as one
  quoted argument (its own flags would otherwise be read as snowglobe's), on a native
  instance's serial root shell, whatever its app is, with the app's environment: its output and
  exit status (`{"exit", "output", "timed_out", "killed"}` with `--json`). Out of time (default
  300 s), the command and everything it started are killed (exit 124).
- `snowglobe cp <src> <dst>` copies files or directories in or out of a native instance
  (`name:/path` on one side).
- `snowglobe mcp <site | url> [--name N] [--keep] [--log-dir DIR]` serves a site to an agent as an
  MCP server over stdio: an isolated Linux machine with `run_command` (with `timeout_seconds`),
  `write_file` and `read_file`. No Docker, KVM or privileges. Example:
  `claude mcp add sandbox -- snowglobe mcp https://filipecabaco.github.io/snowglobe/python/`
- `snowglobe mcp --daemon` serves the daemon to an agent over MCP (stdio): `status`,
  `list_templates`, `add_template`, `remove_template`, `list_machines`, `up`, `stop_machine`,
  `run_command` (on a `machine`, a fresh fork of a `template`, or a `service`'s replica),
  `write_file`, `read_file`, `snapshot_machine`, `list_snapshots`, `remove_snapshot`,
  `list_services`, `add_service`, `remove_service`, `build` (waits by default), `build_status`,
  `list_builds`, `cancel_build`, `submit_run`, `run_status` (`wait_seconds`), `list_runs`,
  `list_ports`, `check_port`, `recent_events`, `fleet_diff`, `fleet_apply`. Example:
  `claude mcp add snowglobe -- snowglobe mcp --daemon`
- `snowglobe bundle <site | url> [-o FILE] [--target linux|darwin] [--runtime snowglobe-vm]`
  makes a site one executable (snowglobe-vm with the site appended) that takes `run`'s flags, plus
  one-shot jobs: `--workspace DIR --cmd COMMAND [--env K=V] [--env-file JSON] [--timeout SECS]`
  writes DIR into a fresh machine, runs the command, and returns its output, exit status and
  `out/`. `--serve SOCKET --jobs-root DIR` restores once and forks per job; `--server SOCKET` is
  its client.
- `snowglobe daemon [--listen ADDR --token-file F]` is the orchestrator: it keeps templates (a
  site restored once) and machines forked from them, with an HTTP/JSON API on a Unix socket in the
  user cache (`/v1/templates`, `/v1/machines`, `/v1/machines/{name}/jobs`,
  `/v1/templates/{name}/jobs` for a job on a fresh fork), and over TCP for requests bearing the
  token with `--listen`. `SNOWGLOBE_DAEMON=http://HOST:PORT` and `SNOWGLOBE_DAEMON_TOKEN` point
  the CLI at a remote one. A daemon started again takes back what still runs.
  It builds too: `POST /v1/builds {"name","source"|"dockerfile","network","memory_mb","cpus",
  "builder","no_template"}` runs `snowglobe build` (a directory by its full path, an image
  reference, or a Dockerfile's text; Docker when there, else natively for images) and makes the
  site a template; `GET /v1/builds`, `/v1/builds/{id}`, `/v1/builds/{id}/log?follow=1&offset=N`,
  `DELETE /v1/builds/{id}` (cancels, or removes a finished one). A machine's terminal is a WebSocket
  at `/v1/machines/{name}/attach?rows=R&cols=C`. `/v1/metrics?since=MS` is a sample every 5 s for
  an hour (memory, machines, replicas, jobs, latencies) and totals; `/metrics` is Prometheus text.
- `snowglobe template add <site> [--name T] [--max-machines N] [--idle 30m]`, `template ls`,
  `template rm T` (removes its machines too). `--idle` stops the template's server after that long
  with no machine; the next `up` or job restores it (about a second).
- `snowglobe daemon --memory 8G [--wait 30s]` caps what templates and machines take together: a
  machine that doesn't fit waits for room, then is refused (429) with the reason. `up --ttl 1h`
  stops a machine after that long.
- `snowglobe up <template> [--name N] [-p [IP:][HOST:]GUEST]... [--label K=V]...` forks a machine
  in tens of milliseconds, sharing the template's memory: it lasts until stopped, keeps what it
  writes, and the daemon forwards its ports (-p 8000 picks a host port). `sh`, `cp`, `exec`,
  `attach`, `ps` and `stop` reach the daemon's machines like instances.
- `snowglobe snapshot save <machine> [--name S]` saves a machine whole (memory, running processes,
  the files it wrote); `up <template> --snapshot S` starts a machine from it, and
  `template add --snapshot S [--name T]` makes it a template, every machine of which starts there.
  `snapshot ls`, `snapshot rm S`.
- `snowglobe service add <name> --template T [-p [IP:]HOST:GUEST]... [--min 0] [--max 1]
  [--idle 5m] [--concurrency 10] [--state discard|keep]` puts a template's machines behind host
  ports the daemon holds: each connection (or `sh <name>`) goes to a replica started on demand.
  `--min 0` scales to zero: replicas idle for `--idle` stop, and the next request forks one (about
  20 ms to the first answer when the template is a snapshot with its server listening).
  `--state keep` saves the replica before it stops and the next one carries on (max 1);
  `discard` starts each from the template. `service ls`, `service rm <name>`; API
  `/v1/services`, `/v1/services/{name}/jobs`.
- `snowglobe ui [--port 7777] [--no-open]` serves the daemon in a browser on 127.0.0.1 (the link
  carries a session token): the last hour on one time axis, a lane per template with machine
  lifespans, the selection, runs on fresh forks, a terminal on any machine (ghostty-web over
  `/v1/machines/{name}/attach`), builds, and templates, machines, services, snapshots and ports.
- `snowglobe submit <template> '<cmd>' [--timeout S] [--env K=V]...` is fire and forget: the
  command runs once on a fresh fork, thrown away after, and the run's id is printed at once.
  `snowglobe runs [<id> [--wait]] [--json]` lists runs or shows one's output and exit status
  (`--wait` exits with it). API: `POST /v1/runs {"template","cmd","env","timeout"}`,
  `GET /v1/runs`, `GET /v1/runs/{id}`.
- `snowglobe ports [--json]` lists the host ports the daemon holds and where each leads (machine
  or service, guest port, open or at zero); `snowglobe ports check <port> [--ip IP]` says whether
  one is free or what holds it (exit 1 when taken). API: `/v1/ports`, `/v1/ports/check?port=N`.
- `snowglobe events [--json] [--after SEQ]` streams the daemon's events (kind, subject, message:
  machine.up, machine.stopped, machine.expired, service.replica_up, template.asleep,
  template.awake, snapshot.saved, admission.refused, ...), the last 200 first; `snowglobe top
  [--once]` shows it live (memory and budget, templates, services, machines, recent events). API:
  `/v1/events` (server-sent events, `?after=SEQ`), `/v1/stats`.
- `snowglobe apply [-f snowglobe.toml]` gets the daemon to what a fleet file says: `[templates.N]`
  (`site`, or `build` = a Dockerfile directory built first with optional `network`, or `snapshot`;
  `idle`, `max_machines`), `[snapshots.N]` (`template`, `run` = commands that must succeed, `ready`
  = a command retried until it succeeds, `timeout`), `[services.N]` (`template`, `ports`, `min`,
  `max`, `idle`, `concurrency`, `state`, `labels`), `[machines.N]` (`template`, `count`, `ports`,
  `ttl`, `labels`). What changed is replaced with what is made from it; what left the file is
  removed. `snowglobe diff` shows the plan; `snowglobe down [-f F | --name FLEET]` removes it all.
  Example: examples/fleet/snowglobe.toml.
- `snowglobe attach <name>` joins a running instance (ctrl-] detaches); `snowglobe ps` lists them;
  `snowglobe stop <name>` stops one (natively: through its stop file, killing its job and logging
  why).
- `snowglobe warm <site> <reads.json ...>` adds the files runs recorded to the site's warm pack.
- `snowglobe tools` builds or finds the tools image; `snowglobe version`.

## Build flags (and the image labels they override)

- `--cmd CMD`: the program to run (default: the image's ENTRYPOINT + CMD). Drops the image's ready and exercise labels.
- `--ready TEXT` / `snowglobe.ready`: snapshot once this text appears on the console (default: after 5 s of quiet).
- `--title TEXT` / `snowglobe.title`: the page title.
- `--memory MB` / `snowglobe.memory`: guest RAM (default 512).
- `--cpus N` / `snowglobe.cpus`: guest CPUs, 1 to 8 (default 1); each runs in a Web Worker.
- `--exercise CMD` (repeatable) / `snowglobe.exercise` (JSON array): commands typed after the snapshot; the files they read are preloaded.
- `--warm REGEX` / `snowglobe.warm`: extra guest paths to preload.
- `--network fetch` / `snowglobe.network`: give the guest a network (default `none`).
- `--tunnel [HOST:]PORT=URL` (repeatable) / `snowglobe.tunnels`: carry other TCP over a WebSocket.
- `--tunnel-token URL` / `snowglobe.tunnel-token`: a fresh token per tunnel connection, put where the URL says `{token}`.
- `--allow-private`: let the build's snapshot reach loopback and private addresses.
- `--builder docker|native`: build with Docker (default) or with none.
- `--sandbox`: keep the guest's file cache in the snapshot, for bundles and native runs.
- `--no-chunks`: don't split large files into content-defined chunks.

Example Dockerfile labels:

    LABEL snowglobe.title="My app" snowglobe.ready="iex(1)> " snowglobe.memory="640" \
          snowglobe.network="fetch" snowglobe.exercise='["h Enum.map"]'

## Networking (`--network fetch`)

Every request leaves as the visitor's own browser request; there is no proxy server.

- HTTP (port 80): each request becomes a fetch().
- HTTPS (port 443): the machine terminates TLS 1.3 itself (armless's web relay) with a per-build CA
  that only the guest trusts, then the request is replayed with fetch("https://...").
- WebSockets (ws://, wss://): the guest's upgrade opens a browser WebSocket; messages pass through.
- Other TCP: only to destinations the site tunnels (`--tunnel`), over a WebSocket.
- In `snowglobe run`, the same requests leave from the host or the container (through
  HTTPS_PROXY/HTTP_PROXY if set); other TCP connections are made directly; private addresses are
  refused unless `--allow-private`.
- Limits in the browser: CORS applies (servers without it answer 502), no raw TCP or UDP.

## Isolation

The guest is an emulated machine whose only ways out are its terminal, its 9p filesystem (read
from the site, written to memory) and, with a network, the web relay. Around the emulator: in the
browser, the page's sandbox; natively, the process's own sandbox (no new programs or processes,
no files beyond the site, its cache, socket, logs and a job's workspace); in Docker, the container
as well. `SNOWGLOBE_SANDBOX=strict` refuses to run without the whole native sandbox.

The shared memory image is kept from changing under a machine: the cache's `ram/` is 0700 and
its files 0444, written under a temporary name and renamed into place, and checked on the open
descriptor before mapping (a regular file of this user's, no write bits, one link, no symlink);
anything off and the run restores the usual way. A page a machine writes is its own, and every
restore and fork gets fresh randomness (the guest kernel reseeds on it).

## What a built site contains

- `index.html`: the page that restores the snapshot (`?embed` hides the status strip).
- `system/state.bin.zst`: the snapshot; `system/filesystem.json` + blobs: the root filesystem over 9p.
- `system/warm.pack`: files preloaded in one request; `warm-report.json` explains what went in.
- `run.json`: measured facts of the build; `transcript.json`: the exercise commands and their output.
